endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: apply output filtering for generative AI.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Track and document instances of anthropomorphization (e.g., human images, mentions of human feelings, cyborg imagery or motifs) in GAI system interfaces.

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations in Personal Health Large Language Models
endorsements.quote: PH-LLMs should therefore be excluded from foundation-model training or fine-tuning by default unless explicit user authorization is obtained, and consent materials should transparently disclose the technical limits of deletion.

evidence.title: When Patients Say “Do Not Share”: LLMs Misroute Sensitive Information in Clinical Documentation
evidence.effect: Routing workflow reduced disclosure from 21.7% to 1.2% without increasing harmful omission.
evidence.quote: On Llama 3.3 70B, the routing workflow reduced disclosure from 21.7% to 1.2% without increasing harmful omission.

evidence.title: Client-Side Ephemeral De-Identification of Protected Health Information (PHI) in Multi-Center Clinical Trial Analysis and Large Language Model Workflows: Validating Zero-Trust Data Sanitization Under HIPAA Safe Harbor Section 164.514(b)
evidence.outcome: PHI detection recall and latency of client-side de-identification before LLM API transmission, versus cloud DLP proxy
evidence.effect: ZTDS achieved 99.94% recall on direct HIPAA 18 identifiers with 1.84 ms latency per note, versus 242.6 ms for cloud DLP proxy; zero outbound PHI bytes in network packet inspection.
evidence.quote: In a benchmark evaluation across 2,500 synthetic multi-center clinical notes containing dense, co-occurring PHI entities (names, medical record numbers, dates, geographic subdivisions, biometricidentifiers, device identifiers, and contact vectors), the client-side ZTDS engine achieved a 99.94% recall rate on direct HIPAA 18 identifiers with an average processing latency of 1.84 ms per standard clinicalnote (mean length: 1,420 characters).

evidence.title: Evaluating privacy leakages in LLM-driven ambient clinical documentation
evidence.outcome: Third-party information leakage in LLM-generated notes with a separate privacy-editing step versus single-step generation
evidence.effect: Separating generation and privacy editing further reduced leakage, but only with contextually specific privacy definitions; no single mitigation eliminated leakage, and combined approaches gave the greatest reductions.
evidence.quote: Decomposing generation and privacy editing into separate steps could further reduce leakage, but only when privacy was defined with contextual specificity.

evidence.title: When Patients Say “Do Not Share”: LLMs Misroute Sensitive Information in Clinical Documentation
evidence.effect: disclosed in 722 of 2,113 documents (34.2%); requests reduced disclosure from 46.6% to 34.2%
evidence.quote: Despite the request, models disclosed sensitive information in 722 of 2,113 documents generated for unrelated specialists or employers (34.2%).

evidence.title: K-anonymity decay in multi-turn clinical large language model conversations
evidence.outcome: Simulated patients reaching small-cell re-identification threshold k < 5
evidence.effect: 79.9% (95% CI: 78.8% to 81.0%) reached k < 5 and 86.2% (95% CI: 85.2% to 87.2%) reached k < 11; median 7 steps to threshold
evidence.quote: Of 5,000 randomly sampled patients, 79.9% (3,994; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 78.8% to 81.0%) reached k < 5 at some point during their disclosure sequence, while 86.2% (4,311; 95% CI: 85.2 to 87.2%) reached k < 11 .
evidence.sample_unit: simulated patients sampled from 133,262 synthetic patients

commentary.bottom_line: Three offline and benchmark studies suggest that routing, privacy-editing, and client-side de-identification controls may reduce PHI leakage from generative AI tools, but none tested these controls in live clinical use. The evidence rests on synthetic notes and simulated outputs, so certainty is very low.

perspectives.view: All three tests point in the same direction, but each used simulated outputs or synthetic notes at evidence levels 4 and 5. No study measured leakage in deployed tools or real patient data. Serious indirectness and study design limits lower certainty to very low despite consistent findings.

A routing workflow cut disclosure from 21.7% to 1.2% without increasing harmful omission. Simply asking the model to withhold information lowered disclosure only from 46.6% to 34.2%. No single mitigation eliminated third-party leakage. A separate simulation found 79.9% of patients reached k < 5 in a median of 7 steps, so filtering direct identifiers may leave re-identification risk.

Client-side de-identification reached 99.94% recall on direct HIPAA identifiers at 1.84 ms per note, compared with 242.6 ms for a cloud DLP proxy. Packet inspection found zero outbound PHI bytes. Privacy editing reduced leakage only when privacy definitions were specific to context, which suggests that setup requires local tailoring.

The latency results suggest client-side filtering may add little delay to clinician work. The studies report no data on licensing cost, staffing to tune privacy rules, or how often legitimate content gets blocked. Administrators cannot yet estimate the full cost of adopting these controls at scale from this evidence.

Among the endorsements, only the CHAI playbook directly calls for output filtering, and it rates the practice as a must. The supplied NIST excerpt addresses anthropomorphization, and the ethics commentary addresses consent for model training. Neither speaks directly to data loss prevention controls.

None of the three tests reported the patient populations behind their synthetic or simulated data. No test examined notes from Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency patients, or notes written in languages other than English.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested input and output filtering or data loss prevention in generative AI tools deployed in live clinical workflows. Prospective evaluations should measure leakage in real traffic, re-identification through quasi-identifiers, the rate of wrongly blocked clinical content, and clinician workarounds. They should also report performance on notes from diverse and multilingual patient populations.
commentary.underserved_note: No test included or reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and all relied on synthetic or simulated data. Detection recall for identifiers in non-English or atypically documented notes remains unknown. Organizations serving these patients should validate filters on their own records before relying on them.
